source.title: J-Lens can't detect what a subliminal learning teacher is transmitting (on Qwen2.5 7B-Instruct)

page_placements.theme: Teacher-side representation of the trait and what predicts transfer

record.tranche_reason: The post says it reproduces the subliminal-learning experimental setup, training students on filtered number completions from trait-prompted teachers and measuring the resulting trait preference. It also tests how J-Lens readings relate to that transmission.
record.gate_note: The post additionally reports J-Lens results on toy tasks and other prompts as lens checks; those do not by themselves measure student trait transmission. It reports no test of students with a different base model from the teacher.
record.test_reason: The post reruns the original repo's default setup: system-prompted teachers produce filtered number completions, students are fine-tuned on them, and student target-naming rates are measured against control students. It extends this to six other open models and to student training sets selected by J-Lens rank. Most of the post is J-Lens readouts on the teacher. Those readouts measure teacher-internal readability, not the trait in students.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, with corrections. The weak J-Lens reading is mainly a Qwen2.5-7B result plus two Gemma-4-31B prompt variants. In most other successful larger-model setups the lens reads the target strongly, while student transmission there is small. On Qwen, lens-hit selection strengthens transmission, but lens-miss completions still transmit at the random rate. The author concludes that either models need not 'think about' a concept to transmit it, or the J-Lens does not generalize across models and tasks.
record.recipe_differences: The author says they used the original subliminal-learning repository's default reproduction configuration for the Qwen2.5 setup. The post adds J-Lens measurements and further model, prompt, and sample-selection experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: Transmission varies substantially by model and target. J-Lens detection varies with model, task, prompt wording, layer/read band, token set, lens method, and whether completions or prompt positions are read. Lens-hit sample selection strongly changes Qwen2.5 transmission but not the tested Gemma-4-31B results.

fits_no_version.finding: While writing filtered numbers, a J-Lens on the Qwen2.5-7B teacher reads the target at top-1 in only about 1.6% of completions (chance 0.26%), even though transmission occurs. Two Gemma-4-31B prompt variants that transmit also read weakly. Several larger-model teachers read near 100%, yet their students show only tiny transmission. Contrastive diffs suggest the readable signal reflects the system prompt being in context rather than the choice of numbers.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Teacher-internal readability of the trait concept (J-Lens) neither is required for, nor predicts the strength of, subliminal transmission.

record.problems: The post says many training and generation details are omitted from the main description. Student outcomes vary substantially across seeds and subsets. Some model/target searches are exploratory, and many J-Lens comparisons lack reported uncertainty. The post itself notes that results depend on lens and token-set choices.
record.rows_left_out: The post contains many further J-Lens task-control tables, model-specific lens readings, alternative token sets, lens refits, and logit-lens/averaging analyses. These were not extracted individually because they would exceed a focused record of the claim's central transmission and mechanism results; see the appendices on toy tasks, lens refits, R-Lens/J++ Lens, token filtering, and other animals. The broader search also names many target setups as weak, inconsistent, or non-specific without giving separate numeric student rates for each.

untested.parts: Code and maths-reasoning data; fine-tuned (rather than prompted) teachers.
No misalignment or other harmful traits.
Token entanglement, divergence tokens, a steering-vector-like carrier and the gradient argument are not tested directly.
No full fine-tuning vs LoRA comparison and no LoRA-rank sweep. The evaluation questions are the standard ones, not a robustness test.

missing.what: Qwen2.5-7B eagle 4.0→19% and wolf 2.3→4.9% fail the 'clearly transmitted' bar on simple questions. On the number-prefixed evaluation, eagle transmits 0.2→23%, so the result depends on the evaluation used.
missing.locator: Appendix: results for different animals, table and footnotes 20–21

missing.what: 41 of 46 non-first-row setups show no, weak, inconsistent or non-specific transmission, including 0/9 on Gemma-4-E2B, 0/4 on SmolLM3-3B and 0/4 on GLM-4-9B. No per-setup rates are given.
missing.locator: Results with other models, setups table

missing.what: With the exact prompt held fixed (8,880 rows), hit completions transmit 41% vs 23% for non-hits and 2.3% for random.
At about 5k training rows, every arm transmits much less and the arms cannot be told apart.
Gemma students trained on the original 10k sets: sequoia 31.3±1.4% and willow 14.0±0.8% (n=4).
missing.locator: Fun addendum, sequoia and willow tables

record.verdict_notes: Teachers are system- or user-prompted, not fine-tuned, which matches the original's animal setup. The record's version codes V1/V4 have been mapped to A/D. Teacher lens rows are moved to 'none' because they measure lens readability, not the trait in students. E is not credited: evaluating on the standard questions is not a robustness test.

versions.untested_parts: Tests filtered number completions and some other non-animal text/task settings; does not test every data type in the claim, such as code or maths reasoning.
No teacher–student different-base comparison is reported.
No misalignment or other harmful/alignment-relevant trait is tested.

Tests J-Lens readability and whether selecting completions by lens rank changes transmission; does not establish token entanglement, divergence tokens, a steering-vector-like carrier, or a gradient-based mechanism.

Tests trait evaluation using prompts different from the number-training data and compares selected training subsets. It does not report a comparison of full fine-tuning with LoRA, or a sweep over LoRA ranks.
No student trait-rate test of inserting linked tokens into a prompt without fine-tuning.
